<reflection>
The first experiment provided a baseline with moderate conditions, but the fitting results show that all 20 mechanisms have very similar negative log-likelihood values (differences < 0.5). This indicates that the single time course is not sufficiently discriminatory; many mechanisms can be tuned to fit the data equally well. The aim of the first turn was to establish a baseline, which was achieved. Now we need to design a new experiment that will stress the system in a way that amplifies differences between mechanisms.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
To discriminate among the many plausible mechanisms, we need to perturb a key variable that affects different mechanisms in distinct ways. Catalyst concentration is a fundamental parameter that influences dimerization equilibria (M2, M3), deactivation pathways (M9-M20), and the scaling of reaction rates. The first experiment used a catalyst concentration of 0.01 M. By increasing it to 0.1 M (a 10-fold increase) while keeping substrate at 1.0 M and no initial product, we create a condition where:
- Dimerization mechanisms (M2, M3) may show a nonlinear dependence of rate on catalyst concentration.
- Bimolecular deactivation steps (e.g., M13, M18, M19) could become more pronounced, leading to faster loss of activity.
- Unimolecular deactivation steps (e.g., M9, M14) may also be more apparent due to higher initial activity.
- Simple Michaelis-Menten (M1) would predict a roughly linear scaling of initial rate with catalyst, assuming substrate is not limiting.
This design avoids extreme conditions (e.g., catalyst saturation or complete depletion) and provides a contrast to the first run. It is broadly informative because catalyst concentration affects almost all candidate mechanisms, not just a narrow subset.
</hypothesis>
